title: Risk Analysis Techniques
blurb: Six ways to reason about a risk. Sort each description onto the technique it describes.
source: ISO 31000:2018 §6.4 · IEC 31010:2019 risk assessment techniques · NIST AI RMF 1.0 MAP 5, MEASURE 2
hint: Drag each description onto its technique. Ask what the method is actually built to reveal — a ranking, a causal path, a failure mode, or a measurement.

zones.name: Likelihood × impact matrix
zones.def: Rate probability and consequence, plot on a grid, use it to prioritise. Fast, coarse, and the default in most registers.

zones.name: Bowtie analysis
zones.def: One event in the middle; causes and preventive barriers on the left, consequences and mitigating barriers on the right.

zones.name: FMEA
zones.def: Work bottom-up from each component's failure modes to their effects, scoring severity, occurrence and detectability.

zones.name: Swiss cheese model
zones.def: Harm occurs when holes in successive layers of defence line up. Explains why single-cause explanations of incidents are usually wrong.

zones.name: Harm taxonomy
zones.def: Enumerate categories of harm — allocative, representational, quality-of-service, dignitary, societal — so that assessment is not limited to what is easy to measure.

zones.name: Inherent vs residual
zones.def: Assess risk before controls and again after them. The gap is what the controls are actually buying.

items.label: Each risk is scored 1–5 for probability and 1–5 for consequence, and the product decides where it sits in the register.
items.why: The scoring grid is the standard prioritisation device. Its weakness is that it flattens a rare catastrophic risk and a frequent trivial one into the same cell.

items.label: Risks are plotted on a red/amber/green grid so the committee can see at a glance which need attention first.
items.why: The heat map is a communication tool built on the same two axes. It is for triage, not for understanding causation.

items.label: The method is criticised for implying precision it does not have when the underlying probabilities are guesses.
items.why: Ordinal scores multiplied together produce numbers that look quantitative and are not. Knowing this is what stops a 12 being treated as twice a 6.

items.label: A single top event is placed in the centre, with threat paths and preventive barriers drawn to its left and consequence paths with mitigating barriers to its right.
items.why: The left/right split around one event is the diagram's defining shape, and it makes the preventive/mitigating distinction visible rather than assumed.

items.label: The analysis makes it obvious that three of the four barriers on the left are the same control counted three times.
items.why: Exposing common-mode barriers is exactly what the diagram is good for. A register of controls listed as text hides that dependency.

items.label: Escalation factors are drawn against each barrier, showing the conditions under which that barrier stops working.
items.why: Escalation factors and their own controls are part of the bowtie method. They are how the diagram avoids assuming barriers are always effective.

items.label: Each component is examined in turn for the ways it can fail, and each failure is scored for severity, likelihood of occurrence and likelihood of detection.
items.why: The three-factor score producing a risk priority number is FMEA's signature. It is bottom-up, from component to effect.

items.label: A failure that is severe but reliably detected before it reaches a user scores lower than one that is silent.
items.why: Detectability as an explicit third axis is unique to FMEA among these techniques, and it is why silent failures rank so highly — which suits ML failure modes well.

items.label: The analysis is criticised for handling combinations of simultaneous failures poorly, since it considers each failure mode on its own.
items.why: Single-point-of-failure orientation is FMEA's known limitation. Use it with a technique that models combinations, not instead of one.

items.label: An incident review concludes that no single defence failed catastrophically; four partial weaknesses happened to align on the day.
items.why: Alignment of holes across layers is the model's core claim, and it is why 'who made the mistake' is usually the wrong first question.

items.label: The model distinguishes active failures at the sharp end from latent conditions created much earlier by design and management decisions.
items.why: The active/latent distinction is Reason's, and it is what directs attention to the decisions that pre-loaded the failure.

items.label: The framing warns that adding another layer of defence gives less protection than expected if the new layer's holes are in the same place.
items.why: Correlated defences are the trap. Two reviewers using the same flawed checklist are one layer, not two.

items.label: The assessment separates harms of allocation, where opportunities or resources are withheld, from harms of representation, where a group is demeaned or erased.
items.why: The allocative/representational split is foundational, and representational harm is the one that slips through assessments driven by accuracy metrics.

items.label: The assessment records that a system works measurably worse for one group even though no decision is being denied to them.
items.why: Quality-of-service harm is a distinct category. Without a taxonomy naming it, this finding tends to be filed as an accuracy issue and deprioritised.

items.label: The method exists to stop the assessment covering only the harms that happen to have a metric attached.
items.why: Enumerating categories first, then seeking measurement, is what keeps dignitary and societal harms in scope rather than out of it.

items.label: The risk is assessed twice: once as if no controls existed, and once with the controls operating as designed.
items.why: The before-and-after pairing is the whole technique. The difference is the evidence base for whether a control is worth its cost.

items.label: A control is found to reduce the score by almost nothing, which becomes the argument for removing it and spending the effort elsewhere.
items.why: Comparing the two assessments is how controls that exist only to be listed get identified. A control with no delta is theatre.

items.label: The register records the level remaining after treatment, and it is this level that must sit within appetite before sign-off.
items.why: Residual risk is what is accepted; inherent risk is only ever context. Accepting against the inherent figure is a category error.
